title: Καρκῖνος καὶ ἀλώπηξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 150. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Καρκῖνος ἀναβὰς ἀπὸ τῆς θαλάσσης ἐπί τινος αἰγιαλοῦ μόνος ἐνέμετο.
sentences.tr: Karkinos anabas apo tēs thalassēs epi tinos aigialou monos enemeto.
sentences.l: A crab, having come up from the sea, was feeding alone upon a certain beach.
sentences.n: ἐπί with the genitive is the plain "on" of place. νέμομαι in the middle is what a grazing animal does; used of a crab it is simply feeding over the ground. μόνος, "alone", is predicative with the verb: he was feeding by himself.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ λιμώττουσα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο αὐτόν, ἀποροῦσα τροφῆς, προσδραμοῦσα συνέλαβεν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de limōttousa, hōs etheasato auton, aporousa trophēs, prosdramousa synelaben auton.
sentences.l: And a fox, being famished, when she beheld him, being at a loss for food, having run up, seized him.
sentences.i: And a hungry fox, catching sight of him and having nothing else to eat, ran up and seized him.
sentences.n: Three circumstantial participles hang on the one finite verb συνέλαβεν — the ordinary engine of these fables, where the whole story is built as a chain of participles ending in a single act. ἀπορέω takes the genitive of what is wanting.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ μέλλων καταβιβρώσκεσθαι ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δίκαια πέπονθα, ὅτι θαλάσσιος ὢν χερσαῖος ἠβουλήθην γενέσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de mellōn katabibrōskesthai ephē· « All’ egōge dikaia pepontha, hoti thalassios ōn chersaios ēboulēthēn genesthai. »
sentences.l: And he, being about to be devoured, said: « Well, I at least have suffered just things, since, being of the sea, I wished to become of the dry land. »
sentences.i: And he, on the point of being eaten, said: « Well, I have suffered no more than I deserve, since, being a creature of the sea, I chose to become a creature of the land. »
sentences.n: δίκαια πέπονθα, "I have suffered just things", is the standing Greek way of saying that a man has got what was coming to him. ἔγωγε is ἐγώ with the emphatic -γε, "I for my part". θαλάσσιος and χερσαῖος are the two adjectives the whole fable turns on: belonging to the sea, belonging to the dry land.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ τὰ οἰκεῖα καταλιπόντες ἐπιτηδεύματα καὶ τοῖς μηδὲν προσήκουσιν ἐπιχειροῦντες εἰκότως δυστυχοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi ta oikeia katalipontes epitēdeumata kai tois mēden prosēkousin epicheirountes eikotōs dystychousin.
sentences.l: So too those of men who have left behind their own pursuits and set their hand to things that belong to them in nothing fare badly, and with reason.
sentences.i: So too those men who abandon their own callings and take up things that are nothing to them come to grief, and deservedly.
sentences.n: The partitive genitive τῶν ἀνθρώπων stands ahead of the article, "those of men who…", a shape these morals use constantly. ἐπιχειρέω, "put the hand to", takes the dative. μηδέν rather than οὐδέν because the persons are a general class, not a set of men one could point to. εἰκότως is "as one would expect".
